newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Trouble ahead of Cyprus's peace concert.
newsitem.headline: Trouble ahead of Cyprus's peace concert.

text.p: Hardliners on both sides created disturbances on Monday in advance of a United Nations-sponsored bicommunal peace concert in Cyprus along the line that has divided the capital for decades.
Up to 400 Greek Cypriot motorcyclists and supporters clashed with Cypriot police protecting access to the site in the heart of Nicosia, witnesses said.
They reported police using batons and guard dogs drove them back. Some demonstrators responded by throwing rocks and witnesses said there appeared to be a few injuries.

On the Turkish side, witnesses reported far-right Turkish "Grey Wolf" nationalists threw stones at the bus carrying Turkish singer Burak Kut to perform. Windows were broken but there were no injuries, they said.
Police had mounted a massive security operation in the capital to ensure the concert remained peaceful. U.N. soldiers checked those entering.
"We have taken all indicative security measures and all access points to the concert venue are controlled," Cyprus police spokesman Glafcos Xenos told Reuters.
Pop stars Burak Kut of Turkey and Sakis Rouvas of Greece were to sing to a crowd of around 5,000 young people in the U.N.-controlled no-mans-land.
The aim was to break the ice, or begin to thaw it, between the youth of the island's two communities separated by years of enmity and mistrust.
Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 in an invasion sparked by a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
The concert has taken on a political meaning in the face of angry reactions from various groups on both sides of the divide.
A far-right Turkish nationalist group drove around the Turkish section of Nicosia on Monday afternoon with loudspeakers publicising a protest meeting against the concert for the evening.
In the south, some Greek Cypriot groups who see the concert as an act of defeatism and an attempt to peddle Turkish propaganda planned a protest a mile (two km) from the concert.
Turkey's Kut arrived in northern Cyprus on Sunday and was met by fans with flowers. He told reporters the concert was to deliver a message of peace and friendship.
"I believe that not just countries but individuals too should refrain from being angry with each other," he said.

Rouvas's arrival in Cyprus, in contrast, was kept a secret. He appeared around midday on Monday in Nicosia looking conspicuous in dark sunglasses along with the rest of his entourage. He didn't talk to reporters.
Turkish Cypriots snapped up all 3,000 free tickets allocated to their community.
But the chance to see Rouvas -- one of Greece's hottest rock stars -- for free did not appear to appeal to many Greek Cypriots.
The United Nations were forced to expand their ticket distribution network to allocate their tickets, and still only managed to get rid of 2,000 of the 3,000 on offer.
